weekly_summary: Week of April 06, 2026 The post that stopped everyone's scroll this week came from Reddit user IM_DaWarez: 95 lbs lost, A1C dropped from 7.4 to 4.1, off six medications, and now done with his doctor entirely. His take — that medicine shifted from treating causes to treating symptoms — hit a nerve. 388 upvotes and a comment section full of people sharing their own med exits. Across the sub, the pattern kept repeating: 20 lbs in two months, a woman whose period returned after just 11 days on carnivore, and one person who finally pulled the trigger on a whole NY strip loin at Costco and hasn't looked back. The most relatable post of the week? Someone complaining that the most annoying part of carnivore is running out of clothes. On YouTube, the electrolyte supplement conversation got a reality check. Dr. Tony Hampton's deep-dive into LMNT, Re-Lyte, and Keto Chow drew 22,000 views and lit up the comments — turns out a lot of people are quietly annoyed about the maltodextrin in popular electrolyte formulas. The top comment was from someone mixing their own for pennies: 400mg magnesium glycinate, potassium citrate, half a teaspoon of Celtic salt, 32oz of water. Meanwhile the protein debate is heating up after Kent Carnivore tackled the "low protein is healthiest" claim that's been circulating in longevity circles. The human stuff matters too. Ground Beef Chief introduced his girlfriend to 174 comments worth of people losing their minds with joy. Week 74 of his journey, and the comment "your heart rate was high cos you're in love" got 20 likes. That's carnivore in 2026 — people aren't just losing weight, they're getting their lives back. Which brings me to you: has carnivore changed something unexpected for you, outside of the scale? Drop it in the comments.

key_insights:
# Marcus's Weekly Carnivore Content Analysis

## What the Numbers Say

37 videos tracked this week across 31 creators. Total reach: **204,458 views**, **19,804 likes**, **2,257 comments**. Average views per video: **5,525**. The range is brutal — top video pulled 29,700 views while the bottom scraped single digits. The top 5 videos by views account for ~49% of all views this week, which means a small number of creators and formats are dominating attention.

Engagement rate tells a different story than raw views. The highest-engagement video this week — Ground Beef Chief's weight loss + love story — hit **28.4% engagement on 1,884 views**. The Carnivore Pensioner's survey video came in at **11.6% engagement on 3,357 views** with 110 comments — exceptional comment density, signaling active audience participation rather than passive consumption.

## This Week's Signal

Three content formats are winning this week:

1. **Recipe content (high-volume, lower engagement)** — high reach, lower comment density. These drive discovery, not community.
2. **Identity/community content (lower views, high engagement)** — Ground Beef Chief (love story), The Carnivore Pensioner (struggle survey). These videos generate comments, not just clicks. People are talking, not just watching.
3. **Controversy/credibility content** — Dr. Tony Hampton's LMNT/electrolyte critique pulled 22,053 views and 235 comments. That comment count is the second-highest in the dataset. Questioning popular products = engagement engine.

## The Opportunity

The comment sections on the identity-driven videos are full of people looking for permission and community — not more macros. Content that validates the psychological experience of doing carnivore in a mainstream world converts at a higher rate than protocol content. The controversy angle (electrolytes, supplements, protocol myths) is also underserved in written form — Dr. Hampton's video is getting 22K views asking hard questions about LMNT but that article doesn't exist yet at a credible editorial level.

qa_section.question: Should I use LMNT or make my own electrolyte mix on carnivore?
qa_section.answer: Both work, and which one you choose comes down to cost, convenience, and how dialed-in your needs are. LMNT's ratios (1000mg sodium, 200mg potassium, 60mg magnesium per packet) are well-matched to what most people lose on a low-carb diet — the kidneys excrete sodium more aggressively when insulin is low, and potassium and magnesium follow. A homemade mix using food-grade sodium chloride, No Salt or Nu-Salt (potassium chloride), and magnesium glycinate or malate powder can replicate those ratios at a fraction of the cost. The case for LMNT is consistency: each packet is pre-measured, which removes the risk of accidentally over-supplementing potassium — the one electrolyte where excess can cause cardiac arrhythmia. Either way, prioritize sodium first (most people need 3-5g/day on carnivore), get adequate potassium from food (ribeye, ground beef, and salmon all contribute meaningfully), and use magnesium supplementally since it's genuinely hard to get enough from muscle meat alone.

citations.title: Dietary sodium and health: more than just blood pressure
citations.authors: Farquhar WB, Edwards DG, Jurkovitz CT, Weintraub WS
citations.summary: Reviews sodium's systemic roles beyond blood pressure regulation, relevant to why low-carb dieters have elevated sodium needs.

qa_section.caveats: People with kidney disease or cardiac conditions should not self-manage electrolytes without physician guidance. If you experience muscle cramps, palpitations, or persistent fatigue on carnivore, get a comprehensive metabolic panel before guessing at supplement doses.

qa_section.question: Does protein amount actually matter on carnivore, or can I eat as much as I want?
qa_section.answer: Protein amount does matter, but not in the way the "low protein is healthiest" crowd suggests. The research is clear that adequate protein (roughly 1.2-1.6g per kilogram of body weight daily, higher toward 2.0-2.4g/kg if you're training or over 60) protects lean mass, supports satiety hormones, and is associated with better metabolic outcomes. On carnivore specifically, protein is your primary source of both essential amino acids and a significant portion of your micronutrients — so undereating it in pursuit of some theoretical longevity benefit is a real risk without strong evidence. The gluconeogenesis concern (that protein converts to glucose and kicks you out of ketosis) is largely overstated: gluconeogenesis is demand-driven, not supply-driven.

citations.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults
citations.authors: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, et al.
citations.summary: Establishes protein intake thresholds for lean mass preservation and gain, with diminishing returns beyond approximately 1.62g/kg/day in resistance-trained adults.

qa_section.caveats: Individuals with pre-existing kidney disease should consult a nephrologist before adopting high-protein intakes. People over 65 consistently benefit from the higher end of the protein range to counteract age-related muscle loss.

qa_section.question: My HbA1c came back elevated on carnivore and my doctor is worried about prediabetes. Should I be?
qa_section.answer: Probably not — but you need the full picture, not just that single number. HbA1c measures how much glucose has attached to your hemoglobin over approximately 90 days. On very low carbohydrate diets, red blood cells tend to live longer because they experience less oxidative stress from glucose exposure. Older red blood cells have simply had more time to accumulate glycation even when your actual blood glucose is well-controlled. The right response to an elevated A1c on carnivore isn't to add carbohydrates back — it's to add context. Request a fasting glucose alongside the A1c. If your fasting glucose is under 100 mg/dL and your post-meal spikes on a CGM are modest and return quickly to baseline, the elevated A1c is almost certainly a measurement artifact of red blood cell longevity, not evidence of glucose dysregulation.

citations.title: Erythrocyte lifespan and glycated hemoglobin: a review
citations.authors: Virtue MA, Furne JK, Nuttall FQ, Levitt MD
citations.summary: Establishes the mechanistic link between red blood cell survival time and HbA1c values, foundational to understanding why A1c can be misleading as a standalone marker.

qa_section.caveats: If your fasting glucose is also elevated (above 110-126 mg/dL consistently), that changes the picture and warrants a proper clinical conversation. People with a family history of type 1 diabetes should also rule out LADA if A1c trends upward over time on carnivore despite adherence.
